title: Residency and Habitat Use of Juvenile Green Turtles in a Protected Coastal Wetland in the Gulf of Oman, United Arab Emirates
content:
ABSTRACT

Coastal wetlands are critical tropical biodiversity hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including marine turtles. Yet they are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, creating an urgent need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands. Using fine-scale GPS telemetry, we quantified residency and habitat use of juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) within a coastal wetland and Ramsar site that has been heavily altered by development but is now protected under the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, Sharjah, United Arab Emirates' Gulf of Oman coast. Juvenile turtles were found to be highly resident, typically remaining within 3 km of the wetland entrance and spending over 80% of their time inside the protected area, confirming its importance as developmental habitat. Spatial and behavioural analyses revealed a strong reliance on artificial habitats, with manmade basins having five times higher odds of use than natural mangrove channels. This basin provides clear ecological value, functioning as a nocturnal refuge and likely foraging habitat, with 77% of core use areas occurring within it. Extending protections to channels linking tidal and oceanic habitats could further improve conservation outcomes, as turtle occupancy followed clear tidal patterns in these corridors. Overall, our findings demonstrate both the importance of coastal wetlands for juvenile turtles and that engineered environments can provide valuable novel habitat, providing connectivity, ecological integrity and resilience are explicitly maintained and integrated into their design.
